assessment:
This study by Wang et al. represents a significant technical and biological advance in whole-organism drug discovery. The authors developed ARQiv-HTS, the first truly high-throughput screening platform for vertebrate models, by integrating automated reporter quantification (ARQiv) with custom robotics. They applied this system to screen over 500,000 transgenic zebrafish larvae against 3,348 compounds from the Johns Hopkins Drug Library (JHDL), testing each at six concentrations with 16 replicates per condition—implementing quantitative HTS (qHTS) principles for the first time in whole-organism screening. The goal was to identify FDA-approved drugs that increase pancreatic β-cell mass, a critical therapeutic target for diabetes.

The screening campaign yielded 225 initial hit compounds (6.7% hit rate), which were systematically triaged and validated through orthogonal assays using complementary transgenic reporter lines. The authors confirmed 24 drugs as leads: 11 compounds that induce endocrine differentiation (Lead I) and 15 that stimulate β-cell proliferation (Lead II), with two compounds showing both activities. Notably, 75% of validated leads are already FDA-approved, facilitating potential clinical translation. The validation rate of 62% is exceptionally high for HTS campaigns, supporting the value of whole-organism screening in reducing false positives. Compared to their prior manual screen of the same library, ARQiv-HTS increased hits implicated nearly threefold (177 vs 62) and leads validated fourfold (24 vs 6), demonstrating the power of the high-throughput approach.

Beyond drug discovery, the study provides important mechanistic insights into pancreatic β-cell biology. Through systematic investigation of shared mechanisms among validated leads, the authors discovered novel roles for two signaling pathways. First, they demonstrated that NF-κB signaling regulates endocrine differentiation: multiple NF-κB inhibitors targeting different pathway steps all induced precocious secondary islet formation, and NF-κB reporter activity co-localized with Notch-responsive pancreatic progenitors. Second, they established that serotonergic signaling selectively stimulates β-cell proliferation. Multiple serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin itself increased β-cell numbers, with paroxetine showing cell-type specificity (increasing β cells but not δ cells). EdU labeling confirmed direct proliferative effects independent of glucose level changes. Critically, these findings were validated across species: paroxetine increased β-cell proliferation in adult zebrafish (3.7-fold) and neonatal mice (at both P14 and P21), demonstrating evolutionary conservation and strengthening translational relevance.

The study's strengths include rigorous statistical design (power calculations, appropriate sample sizes, SSMD scoring), comprehensive validation using orthogonal assays and independent transgenic lines, mechanistic follow-up of implicated pathways, and cross-species validation in mammals. The ARQiv-HTS platform demonstrates exceptional sensitivity (detecting as few as 10 additional β cells) while maintaining objectivity through automated quantification. However, some limitations warrant consideration. The clinical relevance of serotonergic signaling for diabetes remains uncertain given controversial associations between SSRIs and diabetes in humans. The promiscuity of neuromodulator drugs suggests additional mechanistic complexity requiring investigation. While the NF-κB findings are compelling, the functional relationship with Notch signaling requires further characterization. Additionally, 131 compounds with moderate SSMD scores (1.3-1.74) await evaluation, suggesting the full potential of the screen has yet to be realized. The study would also benefit from longer-term functional assessments of β-cell maturation and insulin secretion capacity.

Overall, this work makes fundamental contributions on multiple fronts: it establishes a transformative technology platform for whole-organism HTS, identifies numerous candidate drugs for diabetes therapy with strong translational potential, and reveals novel biology regarding inflammatory and neurotransmitter regulation of pancreatic development. The findings will be of broad interest to researchers in drug discovery, diabetes, developmental biology, and regenerative medicine. The rigorous methodology, high validation rates, and cross-species confirmation provide strong confidence in the main conclusions, though some aspects of therapeutic translation require additional investigation.
